paper_title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.

Stage 1 tests each kind of choice alone, and Stage 2 tests the passing delegations together on new tasks. These were the tool and argument cascades and reflection trigger. Decision models such as JEV (Almeida, 2026) and its open counterparts (InternLM, 2026; StartLuxLabs, 2026; razorback16, 2026) make such choices directly. Given the task, the history and one multiple-choice question, decision model returns probability for each listed option instead of generating text, much like the fast, intuitive System 1 rather than the slow, deliberate System 2 (Kahneman, 2011). In one recorded episode, call to JEV took 28% of an LLM calls time and 2.6% of its price. Existing systems use decision models for game actions, memory, escalation and judging (Ma et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026; Wu and Lim, 2026b; Li et al., 2026). Because harness lists the actions at each step, it can delegate choice to decision model when that model is confident and otherwise defer to the LLM (Figure 1). We call this decision modeling for agents (Chen et al., 2025). Decision models, however, are built and tested on fixed questions and do not adapt to the agent they serve. Whether one works inside an agent has not been tested. Routers and cascades (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025), small function-calling models (Zhang et al., 2025c; Lin et al., 2025) and fast slow agents (Lin et al., 2023; Christakopoulou et al., 2024) also move work away from the large model, and they too have been tested on fixed questions or on single kind of choice, and agent benchmarks score only whole tasks. Inside an agent, decision models mistakes carry over to later steps (Zhu et al., 2025), and one choice changes the next. It also faces states that follow the agents own errors, which fixed question sets rarely contain, and every query to it adds latency. We therefore ask: How can an agent harness delegate routine choices to fast, cheap decision model when the model is reliable, so that agentic tasks become faster and cheaper with little loss of success? Our hypothesis is that decision model helps an agent when it is chosen by tests inside the agent, used only when it is confident, and trained on the states that the agent itself reaches. We build one part for each of these three conditions (Figure 2). AGENTDECISIONBENCH tests decision models at three levels, each closer to real use: on isolated questions with no agent around, at each step of recorded agent runs, where answers are scored but not carried out (step level), and in control of running agent, where each choice changes what comes next (task level). We use public benchmarks and DECISIONGYM, an environment we built that knows the acceptable next steps at every state, so that each choice can be scored. JEVAGENTHARNESS lets an existing harness put each routine choice to decision model as typed multiplechoice question and uses the answer only when the models confidence clears threshold fitted on the agents own trajectories. AGENTDECISION-4B is an open 4B decision model that learns from JEVs answers on the states the agent visits. We will release all three. AGENTDECISION-4B chooses better than JEV inside the agent: on tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them when AGENTDECISION-4B made its tool choices and 82.0% when JEV made them. sections.title: 2 Where and How to Delegate
sections.content: Whether choice is worth handing to the decision model depends on which choice it is and on how the decision models answer is combined with the LLMs. We define the task (Figure 3) and derive rule for what to delegate (2.1). The setup applies to any harness that can list its options at step. Decision points. An episode is one agent run on task, and its state holds what the agent knows at step. decision point is kind of choice that recurs across steps and whose options Od(s) the harness can list. We study eight decision points (Figure 3a). Three choose what the agent does: the tool, its arguments and, without tools, the next action. Five control the loop: whether to write memory, reflect after failure, stop, or route the step to cheaper LLM, and which stored notes to read back. Decision models. decision model reads as text with one question and its options (App. B.3) and returns probability p(o s) for each option. Its answer is the likeliest option, and its confidence c(s) is that options probability (JEV (Almeida, 2026) returns this probability directly). Open models like Intern-Decision and AGENTDECISION4B score all options in one forward pass. Who decides. An integration mode fixes who proposes an answer and who has the last word (Figure 3b). We mostly use the cascade ( CASCADE): the decision model answers first, and the harness uses it when its confidence clears threshold, c(s) τd. Otherwise the LLM decides as usual. In the other modes, the decision model always decides ( REPLACE), shortlists options for the LLM ( ASSIST), approves or rejects the LLMs choice ( GUARD), or decides whether an optional step such as reflection runs ( TRIGGER). We implement all 40 pointmode combinations (App. A). decision point with its mode and threshold is delegation, such as the tool-choice cascade. We seek the cheapest set of delegations whose success stays within 3 points of the LLM alone. example. Consider decision-making customer-service agent asked to cancel an order (App. Figure 6). At each step, the harness asks which of 69 tools to call. At step 3, JEV split its vote between asking the customer (0.63) and cancelling (0.37), so the LLM decided and asked. At step 4, JEV was confident about cancelling the order. JEV then chose the order from options copied from the chat and the reason from fixed list. Both answers were confident, so the call ran without the LLM. An unsure answer or free-text argument would cost one LLM call.

sections.title: 2.1 Deciding what to delegate
sections.content: A threshold rule. Handing choice to the decision model can save an LLM call but may lead to wrong choice. If its confidence equals its chance of being right (App. A), handing over is worth it exactly when c(s) qL C/V , where qL is how often the LLM gets this choice right, the price of the saved call and the cost of wrong choice. This value is the best threshold τd. The decision model may thus be little less accurate than the LLM as long as the saving covers the extra risk. 3 Fitting thresholds. We first run the agent on separate tasks (150 per agent LLM) while the decision model answers every question silently (shadow mode). From these trajectories we estimate, per decision point, how often the LLM was right (qL), calls price (C) and , the drop in task success after one wrong choice, valued at $1 per solved task. The trajectories also give the decision models accuracy at each confidence, so the threshold is the lowest confidence above which accepting is worth it, and the confidence need not match its exact chance of being right (App. A). If none qualifies, the LLM keeps deciding. With JEV and Flash, the fitted thresholds were 1.00 for tools and 0.99 for arguments, so only near-certain answers are used.

sections.title: 3 AGENTDECISIONBENCH
sections.content: A decision model can score well on test and still fail inside an agent. Existing tests ask single questions with fixed answers, so wrong answer never affects what happens next. Agent benchmarks run whole tasks but report only whether task succeeded, without showing which choice went wrong. AGENTDECISIONBENCH tests decision models at three levels on public data and on DECISIONGYM, with every call priced and timed (App. F, Table 5). L1: isolated questions. The decision model answers single questions with no agent around it. We turn the 1,114 tool-choice and 1,949 argument items of BFCL v4 (Patil et al., 2025) and the 928 When2Call items (Ross et al., 2025) into multiplechoice questions. L2: step level, on recorded agent runs. The decision model answers at each step of recorded agent runs, but its answer is only scored, so the run continues as recorded and one mistake cannot cause the next, as when driving policies are tested on recorded drives. Each answer is checked against an answer key of acceptable next steps. All models answer the same 5,314 states of 200 new DECISIONGYM tasks (the common states). L3: task level, in control of the agent. The decision model now makes every tool choice of running agent (every action in ALFWorld) with no threshold, while the LLM writes the arguments, and each choice is carried out. wrong choice changes what the agent sees next, so mistakes can pile up. This level measures task success. It is the hardest level and the closest to deployment. Our agent loop runs τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2026), ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021) and DECISIONGYM tasks, and hooks let us test existing harnesses without changing their code: miniSWE-agent and SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024), and the pi terminal agent on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Terminal-BenchScience (Merrill et al., 2026; Terminal-BenchScience Team, 2026). Levels 2 and 3 need an environment that knows which next steps are acceptable at every state an agent can reach, including after its own mistakes. Public agent benchmarks check only the final state or the progress of run (Lu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2024), have fixed set of tasks and are slow and costly to rerun. We therefore built DECISIONGYM, simulated customer service desk for small shop, with typed tools over small database as in τ -bench (Yao et al., 2025) and requests from templates as in TextWorld (Côté et al., 2019). Every task offers the same 68 tools plus finish in shuffled order: seven core tools, one that asks the customer, 31 near-duplicates of core tools and 29 unrelated ones. Because each task comes from scripted plan, DECISIONGYM derives an answer key at every reachable state from which the task can still be solved, even after detours. Training, threshold fitting and testing use disjoint random seeds. Near-duplicate distractor tools and must-ask states, where the right move is to ask the customer, make the tasks hard. The answer key is hidden from all models, and in strict mode any change to the shops data that is not in the plan ends the episode (App. B). Two further task sets, added after the main study, test the models beyond their training data. Shifted tasks (DECISIONGYM-Shift, App. G.9) rename the tools and change the wording and kinds of requests. Hard tasks (DECISIONGYM-Hard, App. D.6) have 10 or 12 customers each and new rule for cancelling or shipping.

sections.title: JEVAGENTHARNESS
sections.content: JEVAGENTHARNESS moves harnesss routine choices to decision model. It poses each listed choice as multiple-choice question and uses the answer only when the model is confident enough. Otherwise the LLM decides as usual. The harness has three parts (App. Figure 8). typed decision interface. Every choice uses JEVs input format, whose options are the tools, fixed-list or yes/no argument values, or text spans to copy from the context. tool call is split into 4 tool choice and one choice per such argument, so the decision model can pick both while the LLM writes only free text. Any model that accepts this format can be used (App. C). confidence threshold fitted on trajectories. Each decision point gets the threshold of 2.1, fitted on shadow-mode trajectories, so the decision model takes only choices it makes reliably. Below the threshold the LLM decides, so an unsure answer wastes one cheap decision-model call but does not risk the task. Thresholds are refitted when the LLM, decision model or task rules change. Adapters, serving and accounting. Adapters ask the same questions inside existing harnesses through their hooks: strong-or-fast LLM routing in mini-SWE-agent, guards and triggers in pi, and command hooks for Codex CLI and Claude Code. If an adapter or the decision model fails, the harness runs as before (App. Table 9).

sections.title: 5 AGENTDECISION-4B
sections.content: We train our own decision model for two reasons. An API model such as JEV is billed per call and cannot learn harnesss own rules, and off-the-shelf models learn from fixed questions and successful demonstrations. Such data rarely contain the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, where decision model must also answer (App. D.2). We therefore post-train small open model, Qwen3-4B with LoRA (Yang et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2022), on states the harness visits: first by supervised finetuning (SFT), then by RL in the agent loop. Supervised fine-tuning. We run the harness on 587 training tasks and record every decision state s, 15,694 in all. To include states after errors, scripted policy repeats mistakes seen during development (Ross et al., 2011; Laskey et al., 2017), and 30.9% of the states follow mistake (App. D). Where the teacher, JEV, ranks the correct answer first, the target mixes the one-hot label of with the teachers probabilities, ya = α [a = a] + (1 α) pJEV(a s) with α = 0.3. Otherwise the target is the one-hot label alone. SFT fits this target with cross-entropy plus squared-error (Brier) term that keeps the probabilities calibrated: LSFT = Es (cid:80) (cid:2)ya log pa + µ (pa ya)2(cid:3), (1) with pa = pθ(a s) and µ = 0.5. We use LoRA (r=32), 2 epochs and learning rate 104. GRPO inside the agent loop. The SFT model then decides on training tasks while fixed agent LLM does the rest, so it learns from the consequences of its own choices. For each task we run group of = 8 episodes. Episode earns reward for success, Si {0, 1}, reduced for the Ni LLM calls it used, minus penalty when it made an irreversible wrong call (Ei = 1): Ri = Si (cid:0)1 λ min(1, Ni/N0)(cid:1) ηEi, (2) with λ = 0.5, N0 = 10 and η = 0.2, so solved task with ten or more LLM calls earns half. Each episodes advantage is its reward relative to the group, ˆAi = (Ri R)/σR, and every decision at in the episode shares it in the GRPO objective (Shao et al., 2024), plus step-level term at states that recur within the group (Feng et al., 2025a), with KL penalty to the SFT model (App. D). Flash-Lite is the agent LLM, and iteration 15 is kept. Evaluation. Stage 2 swaps JEV for the frozen AGENTDECISION-4B and refits the thresholds. We later trained it further on public tool-use data.

sections.title: 6 Experimental Protocol
sections.content: Stage 1 tests each delegation alone and keeps those that are cheaper and non-inferior to the LLM alone. Non-inferior means that one-sided test at the 5% level, on the same tasks run both ways, shows loss of less than 3 points in task success (5 on τ 2-bench; App. E). Stage 2 tests the passing delegations together on new tasks, because delegations can interact. We pre-registered the models, tasks and tests, and registered the Stage-2 plan before reading any Stage-1 result, so that choosing the combination could not bias its test. Stage 1: each delegation alone. The decision model is JEV (and Intern-Decision-4B for three delegations). The agent LLM is Gemini 3.5 Flash (Flash) with native tool calls. The cheaper, weaker Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (Flash-Lite) receives routed steps, simulates the τ 2-bench user and is second agent LLM on DECISIONGYM (App. F). The LLM alone and simple controls without decision model run on the same tasks as each delegation (App. B.5). With eleven registered tests, few could pass by chance, so Holms method (Holm, 1979) makes each test stricter and keeps the chance of any wrong pass at 5%. Other results are descriptive. 5 the delegations together. script Stage 2: chose the combination by rule fixed in advance. At each decision point it took the delegation that passed Stage 1 with the largest saving, or kept the LLM if none passed (App. E). We ran the combination on 500 new DECISIONGYM tasks and on τ 2-bench telecom tasks. Four Holm-corrected tests check two things. The first two check that the combination still works. It should be non-inferior to the LLM alone at lower cost, and cheaper than its best single delegation without losing success, or combining would not be worth it. The other two check that model we train can take JEVs place. On the common states, AGENTDECISION4B should beat Intern-Decision-4B, model of its size that never saw the agents states, and be non-inferior to its teacher JEV. The combination should also stay non-inferior to the LLM alone when AGENTDECISION-4B replaces JEV.

sections.title: 7.1 RQ1: Do isolated scores predict success?
sections.content: On isolated questions (Figure 4a), JEV was 1.7 points less accurate than Flash at 1/50 of its cost (App. G.6). On one L4 GPU, AGENTDECISION4B and AGENTDECISION-0.8B cost about 4 and 9 times less per decision than JEV (App. G.7). At the task level, the ranking differed from the isolated one (Figure 4b). StartLux-9B was the most accurate model on BFCL tool choice (92.2%), yet it solved only 69.5% of tasks. AGENTDECISION4B was less accurate on BFCL (89.3%) but solved 91.5% of tasks, and JEV solved 82.0%. Step-level accuracy ranked the models nearly as task success did (Kendall correlation 0.84). The gap lies at mustask states, where AGENTDECISION-4B answered 67.4% correctly and JEV answered 58.3%. Finding 1. Isolated scores misrank decision models. The best decision model on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, while AGENTDECISION4B solved 91.5%.

sections.title: 8 Related Work
sections.content: Decision models. JEV and open models like Intern-Decision, StartLux-Decision and OpenJev (Almeida, 2026; InternLM, 2026; StartLuxLabs, 2026; razorback16, 2026) score listed options, while DecisionFlow (Chen et al., 2025) structures LLM decisions. REFLEX hands an action to the LLM when its confidence falls below one global threshold (Wu and Lim, 2026b), and we fit one per decision point. Decision evaluation. Decision and tool-use benchmarks score fixed questions (Benchmark Heaven, 2026; Ling et al., 2026; Patil et al., 2025; Ross et al., 2025), and agent environments score whole episodes (Yao et al., 2025; Trivedi et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025). Models with equal scores can still decide differently (Zhang et al., 2026). AGENTDECISIONBENCH adds stepand tasklevel tests. Routing, deferral and training. Routers and cascades choose the model for call (Chen et al., 2024; Ong et al., 2025; Aggarwal et al., 2024). Learned routers, compared in LLMRouter (Feng et al., 2026a), use queryLLM graphs, multi-LLM logs or multi-round RL (Feng et al., 2025b, 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025a). decision model instead scores listed options and defers if unsure, like learning to defer (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Mozannar and Sontag, 2020). Agentic RL trains the LLM (Jin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025d), while we train the decision model (App. H).

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: Three failure modes recur. confident wrong choice at an irreversible step ends the task. All 34 of JEVs failed tasks began with an irreversible wrong tool choice, usually cancelling where the agent should have asked. Models trained on agent states made no such error (App. G.7). The decision model can also face new rule. On hard tasks with 10 customers, AGENTDECISION-4B, trained without this rule, made most cancel-or-ship decisions but got only 81.6% of them right, and the agent solved 3.0% of tasks against 88.0% for the LLM alone. Refitting the threshold restored success with Our results support the hypothesis that decision models help agents when tested, used and trained inside the agent. Only tests inside the agent (AGENTDECISIONBENCH) showed which decision models work there. Trained on the agents states, AGENTDECISION-4B beat JEV inside the agent and, with thresholds fitted on agent trajectories (JEVAGENTHARNESS), made most routine choices. Models trained this way made the agent 81.189.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of success.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: All tasks and prompts are in English, and most runs use Gemini agent LLMs, with DeepSeek and OpenAI models in few. With other languages or agent LLMs, other kinds of choices may be worth delegating. Our main tests are non-inferiority tests. They show that task success drops by less than fixed margin (3 points, 5 on τ 2-bench), and showing equal success would need an equivalence test. The thresholds and the trained decision model are fitted to an agents own runs, so new agent, new tools or new task family call for refitting the thresholds and, for the best accuracy, training on that agents states, as we did for ALFWorld. In coding agents, whose actions are free text, the decision model can only choose which LLM writes step. There the savings were small (7.010.5%), and sending the steps that only read files to fast LLM gave no reliable saving, because the decision model could hardly tell those steps from the others (App. C.3). Prices and latencies are those we recorded, and they change with providers, hardware and how the decision model is served (App. F). We did not compare with learned routers such as RouteLLM on the same tasks, and GRPO added no measurable gain over SFT in our runs. In deployment, the share of answers above the threshold could be tracked to notice when the tasks drift and the thresholds need refitting.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: We will release the benchmark, harness, recipes, trained models and data (App. F). Training on JEV outputs and redistributing derived weights depend on the providers terms, and StartLux-Decision weights are licensed CC BY-NC 4.0. All benchmarks are public, and we collect no personal data: DECISIONGYM customers, orders and e-mail addresses are generated from templates. Lower cost can make fast models failures on safety-relevant decisions easy to overlook. With the cheaper FlashLite as agent LLM, the stop guard accepted 40.7% of the LLMs own wrong attempts to end the task (App. Table 7), so decision-model guard should never be the only control on an irreversible action. If an adapter fails, the step runs without it (4). Adapters therefore control only cost and speed and should not be used as security boundaries. We did not test adversarial observations or policy injection, which can flip decision models typed answers (Xu et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Wu and Lim, 2026a), so our results hold for benign states only. Cheaper agent control also lowers the cost of misuse at scale.

Beyond 8, JEV has served as REPLACE for action-only and memory control (Ma et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026) and as judge or monitor (Guo et al., 2026b; Kwartler et al., 2026). Studies examine its calibration and robustness (Deußer et al., 2026; Wu and Lim, 2026a). Closest to us, JEV-as-a-Judge fits an acceptance threshold on about 100 local labels (Li et al., 2026), and REFLEX escalates agent actions below one global threshold, an action-level CASCADE (Wu and Lim, 2026b). We compare decision points and modes under one cost ledger, set thresholds by price, and test the chosen combination and post-trained model on new tasks. Routers, cascades and deferral. Cascade routing (Dekoninck et al., 2025), agentic routers (Liu et al., 2026) and fastslow controllers (Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025b) decide which model or how much thinking step gets. JEV and LLM judges err on the same items, so cascade between them mainly saves cost (Rao and CallisonBurch, 2026). Agents also ask for help through uncertainty-aware deferral (Piatrashyn et al., 2026) or conformal prediction (Ren et al., 2023), and finite-sample risk control (Angelopoulos et al., 2024) could replace our plug-in thresholds, and serving systems such as vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) lower the price of each call. Tool retrieval (Patil et al., 2024) is ASSIST with similarity scorer, as in our BM25 control (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009), and reflection (Shinn et al., 2023) is TRIGGER decision in our terms. Paired replay of recorded states has precedent in search stopping (zilliztech, 2025), and process reward models score agent steps (Xi et al., 2026). AGENTDECISIONBENCH measures the gap directly by scoring the same models on isolated questions, recorded states and live tasks. Training small models on agent states. Agentic RL trains the generating LLM on multi-turn trajectories (Zhou et al., 2024b; Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025d), tool use (Qian et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025) or tool-call efficiency (Wang et al., 2025a). We train the decision model. Open decision models trained on target loop have beaten JEV there (lexmount, 2026) or on static set without transferring (Cheng et al., 2026), and small models are argued to suffice for most agentic calls (Belcak et al., 2026). We compare on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024) with distillation on fixed states (Hinton et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2025) and use group-relative RL (Shao et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025a) with calibration-aware rewards (Damani et al., 2026).
